name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 9 May 1970

clue.text: Dance to an instrumental duet

blocks.note: a duet of instruments: a horn followed by a pipe, two wind instruments side by side

explanation.surface: A dance is being performed to music played by two instrumentalists.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'duet' is literal: two instruments, HORN and PIPE, set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornpipe is a lively solo dance traditionally associated with sailors.

clue.text: Play that seems to expect few houses

blocks.note: first meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy about the Prince of Denmark
second meaning: a small village with only a handful of dwellings

explanation.surface: A theatre production whose producers fear only a small audience will turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' tempts a theatrical reading (a full house), but here it means actual buildings in a tiny settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy shares its title with the word for a small rural settlement lacking its own church.

clue.text: Could there be a more incautious breakfast?

definitions.note: a rasher is one item of a breakfast, a definition by example

blocks.note: first meaning: comparative of rash, meaning reckless
second meaning: a thin slice of bacon fried for the morning meal

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether any morning meal could be more reckless than this one.
explanation.walkthrough: The comparative adjective and the bacon slice are spelt identically.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice of bacon is a staple of the cooked British morning meal, so it stands here by example.

clue.text: He was told to let go

definitions.text: He was told to let go

blocks.clueFragment: He was told to let go
blocks.note: surface reading: someone instructed to loosen a grip on something

blocks.clueFragment: He was told to let go
blocks.note: setter's reading: the Egyptian king to whom Moses said 'Let my people go' in Exodus

explanation.surface: A man was ordered to release his hold.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Exodus Moses repeatedly demanded that the Egyptian king release the Israelites from slavery.

clue.text: Pebble pundit of the people's crossing

definitions.text: Pebble pundit of the people's crossing

blocks.note: setter's reading: the Greek psephos, a pebble, used by Athenians to cast votes, gives this expert his name
surface reading suggests a street crossing; really the people's cross on a ballot paper at an election

explanation.surface: An expert on stones holds forth about a pedestrian crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: This specialist studies elections and voting patterns, his title drawn from the Greek word for a voting pebble.

clue.text: Anger of a militant master of theology

blocks.note: militancy is a warlike state
MTh is the abbreviation for the degree Master of Theology

explanation.surface: A combative theologian is in a temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Heat of feeling, as in speaking with some heat, can describe indignation or passionate displeasure.

clue.text: For a doyen an analgesic

indicators.note: 'for' here means in exchange for: these letters are traded in for a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly senior figure is given a painkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is loose by modern standards; the fodder is the seven letters of 'doyen' and 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne is a medicine that relieves pain, which is exactly what an analgesic does.

clue.text: Such a duck of an official!

blocks.note: first meaning: a brightly coloured East Asian duck
second meaning: a high-ranking bureaucrat, originally in imperial China

explanation.surface: An exclamation of fond exasperation at a bureaucrat, calling him a 'duck'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a term of endearment; it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a colourful Chinese waterfowl and a senior imperial Chinese bureaucrat carry this name.

clue.text: Master Humphrey's study?

blocks.note: surface reading: the private room of a gentleman called Master Humphrey
setter's reading: Dickens's weekly periodical 'Master Humphrey's Clock', so the study of clocks

explanation.surface: A question about the private room of someone called Master Humphrey.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the science of measuring time and of making clocks and watches.

clue.text: In fog a range of sight can be wrong

blocks.note: a thin fog
taken as written
ken is one's range of sight or knowledge

explanation.surface: In foggy weather, how far you can see may be misjudged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in error and having the wrong idea mean the same thing.

clue.text: Mr Chips a marrying man?

blocks.note: first meaning: a carpenter, nicknamed Chips for the wood shavings of his trade
second meaning: one who unites, as a clergyman joins couples in matrimony

explanation.surface: Is the schoolmaster of 'Goodbye, Mr Chips' the type to settle down?
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Chips recalls the novel's schoolmaster, but 'Chips' is old slang for a carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworker making furniture and a person who unites things share this name, from the verb to join.

clue.text: Two feet of accommodation?

blocks.note: surface reading: a measurement of twenty-four inches of space
setter's reading: space where people are accommodated only on their own two feet, as in a full theatre

explanation.surface: A query about lodgings measuring a mere two feet.
explanation.definitionFit: When seats are sold out, a venue may still admit people who must stay upright throughout the show.

clue.text: Humbug for a pupil

definitions.note: a phrase describing what the answer is used for

blocks.note: first meaning: nonsense intended to deceive
second meaning: a lotion for bathing the eye, of which the pupil is part

explanation.surface: A schoolboy is fed nonsense, or perhaps a striped sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil' suggests a schoolchild; it is the dark centre of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Both deceptive talk and a soothing lotion for sore eyes share this compound word.

clue.text: If the marine engine won't start . . .

definitions.text: If the marine engine won't start . . .

blocks.clueFragment: If the marine engine won't start
blocks.note: surface reading: a boat owner's mechanical breakdown
setter's reading: the advice that follows the dots, to rely on canvas instead of the motor

explanation.surface: A sailor's boat motor has failed to fire up.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as TRY SAIL: the natural completion of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small strong fore-and-aft canvas set on a mast in heavy weather.

clue.text: Her lad pining? No consoling himself with others

indicators.note: 'No' rejects the given order of the letters, demanding they be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Her boyfriend is not pining for her; he is seeking comfort with other women.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who flirts and has casual affairs with several women is consoling himself with others.

clue.text: I count the bodices, sir

definitions.note: the answer is a name, that of the knight Sir Isumbras

blocks.note: taken as written
to sum is to add up or count
brassieres, close-fitting underbodices

explanation.surface: A shop assistant or valet reports to his master on a tally of women's garments.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Isumbras is the hero of a Middle English verse romance, so the clue's closing 'sir' completes his title.
explanation.definitionFit: The knight Isumbras, of the medieval romance, is always styled with that title of knighthood.

clue.text: What goes on in the meantime?

definitions.text: What goes on in the meantime?

blocks.clueFragment: What goes on in the meantime?
blocks.note: surface reading: a general question about events happening meanwhile
setter's reading: what is put on the stage between two acts of a play

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is happening while they wait.
explanation.definitionFit: This French theatrical term means an interval between acts, or a piece performed during it.

clue.text: "Sir, we are a nest of " (Johnson)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a gap to fill
setter's reading: Dr Samuel Johnson's boast about the poets of Pembroke College, Oxford

explanation.surface: A quotation from Samuel Johnson with its last words missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson said his Oxford college was full of poets, likened to songbirds in a nest.

clue.text: Describes the contents of a silver casket

definitions.text: Describes the contents of a silver casket

blocks.clueFragment: the contents of a silver casket
blocks.note: surface reading: valuables kept in a box of silver
setter's reading: in The Merchant of Venice the silver casket holds a portrait of a blinking fool

explanation.surface: A description of what lies inside a precious box.
explanation.walkthrough: Portia's suitors choose between gold, silver and lead caskets; Arragon picks silver and finds a fool's portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: The portrait the Prince of Arragon finds is of a fool, so what it shows is foolish.

clue.text: Leave the track for rugged ridges to the south

indicators.note: rugged ground is broken and uneven, so these letters are broken up

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A hiker strays off the path to explore rough hills further south.
explanation.definitionFit: To wander off the subject in speech or writing is to depart from the main path of the argument.

clue.text: Hat to wear with a lounge suit?

definitions.text: Hat to wear with a lounge suit?

blocks.clueFragment: Hat to wear with a lounge suit?
blocks.note: surface reading: headgear matching a man's informal business suit
setter's reading: a soft wide-brimmed hat whose name also means to lounge about

explanation.surface: A man asks which hat goes with his everyday suit.
explanation.walkthrough: The slouch hat, with one side of the brim pinned up, is worn by Australian soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft felt hat with a broad brim takes its name from a word meaning to lounge or droop lazily.

clue.text: A trail up the hill

definitions.note: a phrase, while the answer is a noun for a climb

blocks.note: taken as written
the trail of smell left by an animal for hounds

explanation.surface: A footpath leads up the slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A climb or upward slope is the way up a rise in the ground.

clue.text: Allowances for error spoil the drinks

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
glasses of gin

explanation.surface: Mistakes in mixing ruin the cocktails.
explanation.definitionFit: Margins of error are extra amounts allowed in case of miscalculation.

clue.text: Inability to keep a straight face is wicked in school

definitions.text: Inability to keep a straight face

indicators.note: read as 'given a wick', it says the answer plus that extra ending makes the school's name, so the ending comes off

blocks.note: Giggleswick is a boarding school in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Pupils who cannot stop laughing are being naughty in class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' splits as wick-ed: add WICK to GIGGLES and you get Giggleswick, an English school.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit of uncontrollable laughter stops a person from looking serious.

clue.text: Ire etc, so to speak

indicators.note: 'so' means 'in this way', inviting the letters to be set out in another fashion

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Anger and the like, as it were.
explanation.definitionFit: To recite is to say a piece aloud from memory, a particular way of speaking.

clue.text: Petticoat government?

blocks.note: surface reading: a government run by women
setter's reading: the wife in charge of the household, ruling the domestic roost

explanation.surface: A question about rule by women.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase also names self-government for a region, the great Irish political issue.
explanation.definitionFit: When the woman of the house holds sway, the household is governed domestically by her.

clue.text: The day for the deli cry of natural gas?

blocks.note: surface reading: a delicatessen's special day
setter's reading: what a gas leak announces itself with, a foul odour

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about a delicatessen and a gas supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue appears garbled in the archive; the part about natural gas points to a foul smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong offensive odour is how leaking gas calls attention to itself.

clue.text: Grabber's initial success

blocks.note: surface reading: a thief's first successful job
setter's reading: the first half of a smash-and-grab, followed by a word for a success

explanation.surface: A thief pulls off his first successful raid.
explanation.walkthrough: A smash-and-grab raider breaks a shop window and snatches goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A play, film or song that is hugely popular is a sensational triumph.
